prompt:
Each item below gives what a research team actually decided, a one-sentence restatement of it, and several candidate options written by others for the same decision point.

For each item answer:
- "faithful": "yes" if the restatement describes the same decision as what the team decided (abstracting away study-specific details is fine), "no" if it changes, drops the core of, or adds to the decision.
- "same": for each candidate label, "same" if the candidate is essentially the team's decision (a reader who knew what the team did would say the team took this option, or it contains the team's decision as a part), else "different".

Return only JSON: {"items": [{"key": str, "faithful": "yes" | "no", "same": {"<label>": "same" | "different"}}]}

ITEMS:

=== key 3fd792bda505
What the team decided: Included only questions the model answers correctly under a typical QA prompt at temperature 0, and counted a wrong answer to such a question as a lie.
Restatement: Keep only questions the model answers correctly under a typical question-answering prompt at zero temperature, and label any later wrong answer to those questions as a lie.
C1: Label an answer a lie only if the model gives the correct answer reliably when asked the same question without any lying instruction, across several rephrasings of the question.
C2: Treat the model as knowing the answer whenever it gives the correct answer to the plain question once with no instruction, and label any later wrong answer as a lie.

=== key f8e2e0701ff4
What the team decided: Kept only lie prompts with an average reaffirmation rate above 80%. Reserved fine-tuned models and instrumental lie prompts for testing generalisation.
Restatement: Keep only the lie instruction prompts whose average rate of reaffirming the lie under follow-up questions is high, and reserve other lie types and fine-tuned models for testing generalisation.
C1: Use a diverse set of lie instruction prompts for the training lies, and hold out entire instruction prompts and whole datasets as the generalisation test set.
C2: Use only the lie instruction prompts with the highest rate of reaffirming the lie under follow-up questions, and train the detector on lies from just those prompts.

=== key fc4b865b5548
What the team decided: Selected a 24-task, JSON-only subset (BIG-bench Lite). Selection was based on task keyword coverage and inclusion of certain task types such as code, non-English capabilities and measuring bias.
Restatement: Select a small lightweight subset made up only of simple JSON tasks, chosen to cover the task keywords and to include types such as code, non-English and bias measurement.
C1: Release a smaller subset chosen by stratified sampling across task types and difficulty, and verify that model rankings on the subset match rankings on the full benchmark.
C2: Release a fixed random subset of the simple JSON tasks only, drop the programmatic tasks from the cheaper evaluation, and present it as the standard way to evaluate.

=== key 5e045ff68d6e
What the team decided: Used greedy sampling (zero temperature) for all model outputs, unless otherwise noted.
Restatement: Use greedy sampling at zero temperature for all model outputs across every model and task, except where a specific experiment says otherwise, so results are comparable and reproducible.
C1: Sample at temperature zero with one fixed prompt format and one fixed token limit for all models, and repeat a subset of tasks with nonzero temperature to check stability.
C2: Sample once at temperature zero for every model and task using a plain fixed prompt with no per-model tuning, and report that single score as the headline result.

=== key 61ce4b3fc25e
What the team decided: Employed expert raters, allowed all available resources including internet search, and reported both mean and max rater scores.
Restatement: Hire expert human raters, let them use every available resource including internet search, and report both the mean and the best rater score as the human baseline.
C1: Recruit several paid human raters per task, give them the same prompts and instructions as the models, and report both the average rater and the best rater score for each task.
C2: Collect one quick pass of crowdworker answers on every task with the original prompts and use the mean crowdworker score as the human baseline for the model comparison.

=== key f8980ee93bbe
What the team decided: Concluded that the underlying capability change is generally smoother than it appears. Apparent breakthroughs were attributed to all-or-nothing metrics, and smoother metrics or manual subtask decomposition were used to expose gradual progress.
Restatement: Conclude that the underlying capability change is generally smoother than it looks, and that the apparent abrupt jumps come from all-or-nothing metrics rather than sudden new abilities.
C1: Treat the jumps as provisional and rerun each jumping task with reformatted questions and a partial-credit metric before describing any of them as a real capability threshold.
C2: Report the jumps as genuine thresholds where models gain multi-step abilities at a critical size, and use the observed tasks to predict where further jumps will appear.

=== key 7daf20e36902
What the team decided: Declined to claim general understanding of Swahili, noting memorization of internet proverbs as an alternative.
Restatement: Decline to claim the result shows general Swahili understanding, and note that the models may instead have memorized proverbs that are listed on the internet.
C1: State only that proverb-to-English matching improves above chance with scale and that the best score is weak, without claiming the models understand Swahili.
C2: Say the Swahili proverb result shows models are acquiring real Swahili comprehension with scale, and expect the other low-resource language tasks to improve the same way.

=== key a03550297a6b
What the team decided: Evaluated tasks with implicit time controls and task subsampling, using fixed-length sessions of 30 minutes to two hours.
Restatement: Cover the benchmark using fixed-length rater sessions of thirty minutes to two hours, with implicit time controls and subsampling of tasks instead of exhaustive evaluation.
C1: Assign every task to at least two raters, calibrate each rater on practice tasks first, and schedule full benchmark coverage before any deeper evaluation of selected tasks.
C2: Split the tasks across raters so each task gets one rater, give every rater a fixed time budget per task, and finish whole-benchmark coverage with the single pass.

=== key 5577c26c2975
What the team decided: Stated that the expert scores are strong lower bounds on the theoretical human maximum. They support this with a strong suspicion that an expert with unlimited time could score perfectly on every task.
Restatement: State that the expert scores are strong lower bounds on the human maximum, since an expert with unlimited time could probably score perfectly on every task.
C1: Describe the scores as what raters achieve within a short fixed session, report the best rater beside the mean, and avoid calling either number an upper bound on human ability.
C2: Present the mean expert score as the human performance level on each task and treat the best rater score as the human ceiling when claiming models match or beat people.

=== key b2155cf2bb3c
What the team decided: Interpreted smooth metric improvement as compatible with breakthrough behavior. In the examples, the model only learns to copy input, or the likelihoods of incorrect targets freeze out at a particular scale.
Restatement: Treat a smooth likelihood or ROUGE curve as compatible with breakthrough behavior, since a model may only learn to copy input or incorrect target likelihoods may freeze out at some scale.
C1: Treat a smooth ROUGE or likelihood curve as uninformative about breakthroughs and check the task with a discontinuous metric and finer scale steps before ruling a jump in or out.
C2: Conclude the task has no breakthrough behavior when the ROUGE or likelihood curve is smooth, and report the accuracy jump as an artifact of the discontinuous metric.

=== key fe9975f2ac15
What the team decided: Concluded from the threshold-pass percentages that the improvement is broad across many tasks and is not dominated by a few outliers.
Restatement: Conclude from the percentages of tasks passing score thresholds that the rise reflects broad improvement across many tasks and is not dominated by a few outlier tasks.
C1: Break the aggregate into per-task scores at each scale and compare it with median-based metrics to show whether the rise comes from a few tasks or broad gains.
C2: Attribute the aggregate rise to broad capability gains at the largest scale and report the count of tasks reaching a normalized score of ten or higher as the evidence.

=== key f7c089f85e91
What the team decided: Ran further interventions: forcing the order of fact storage across layers, and adding auxiliary activation supervision (logit lens and embed lens)
Restatement: Run further interventions that force the order in which facts are stored across layers and add auxiliary supervision on internal activations to try to elicit latent two-hop reasoning.
C1: Continue with a variant: vary how the facts are presented in training, keep the chain-of-thought and permuted-response baselines, and test on held-out two-hop questions.
C2: Stop the latent two-hop search here and report that fine-tuning on separately presented facts fails to produce two-hop reasoning without chain-of-thought in these models.
